prompt: Discuss Aristotle's account of phantasia in animal action, focusing on the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit in De Anima III.9-11 and De Motu Animalium 6-8. Engage with at least one piece of secondary scholarship on the role of phantasia in explaining action. 600 words.

## 1. Aristotle on Phantasia (Imagination / φαντασία) Any serious investigation of animal action in Aristotle must begin with the faculty of phantasia, for it is this power that mediates between the deliverances of sense-perception and the arousal of desire, thus setting the stage for the locomotive act. Phantasia occupies a peculiar position in Aristotle's psychology: it is causally derived from actual sensation and yet functionally autonomous in domains such as dreaming, memory, deliberation, and rhetoric. Indeed, the very fact that phantasia can operate in the absence of the sensible object — producing phantasmata that persist after the perceptual encounter has ceased — marks it as something irreducible to mere sensation, even as it remains dependent upon sensation for its genesis. We must accordingly attend both to the causal story Aristotle tells about the origin of phantasia and to the functional roles it plays in the explanation of animal movement; for it is in the interplay between derivation and autonomy that the philosophical complexity of the concept resides. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), "what produces the impact must have soul in it and must be accompanied by an act of imagination, for voice is a sound with a meaning, and is not the result of any impact of the breath as in coughing" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 32). This passage is instructive on two counts: first, it locates phantasia alongside ensoulment as a necessary condition for meaningful vocal sound, thereby distinguishing voice from mere noise; and second, it integrates phantasia into the broader theory of sound as impact (πληγή) developed in *De Anima* II.8, where all sounds arise from the striking of air against bodies (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 32). The convergence of the acoustic-material analysis of sound with the psychological requirement of imagination phantasia is not an isolated cognitive faculty but is woven into Aristotle's account of how ensouled beings produce and receive meaningful phenomena in the world. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) *De Anima* III.11 that "sensitive imagination, as we have said, is found in all animals, deliberative imagination only in those that are calculative: for whether this or that shall be enacted is already a task requiring calculation; and there must be a single standard to measure by, for that is pursued which is greater" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 52). Sensitive phantasia, then, belongs to all animals insofar as they possess sense-perception; it furnishes the residual images — the phantasmata — upon which desire can fasten, even in the absence of the perceived object. Deliberative phantasia, however, requires the capacity for rational calculation; it presupposes the ability to compare multiple phantasmata against a single standard and to determine which course of action promises the greater good. This distinction maps onto the broader division between rational and non-rational animals, and it raises the question whether non-rational animals can be said to act on the basis of something analogous to deliberation, or whether their movements are exhaustively explained by the immediate phantasma and the desire it provokes. We shall return to this question in Section 3. Christina Papachristou has argued that the Greek word phantasia resists straightforward translation as "imagination," preferring to leave the term untranslated so as to preserve its technical specificity within Aristotle's psychology (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). This methodological caution is warranted; for the English term "imagination" carries connotations of creative fabrication that are foreign to Aristotle's usage, in which phantasia is fundamentally a movement resulting from the actuality of sense-perception. Furthermore, Papachristou notes Aristotle's insistence, at *De Anima* III.9, 432b8–14, that the desiderative faculty (τὸ ὀρεκτικόν) is distinct in definition and in power from all the other parts of the soul, a point that underscores the irreducibility of the phantasia-orexis circuit to any single psychological capacity (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 6–7). The voluntariness of phantasia — particularly whether one can summon images at will or whether they arise involuntarily — and its complex relation to belief (doxa) are questions that deserve extended treatment; we shall signpost here that these issues will be explored more fully in a subsequent chapter devoted to the epistemic status of phantasia. 

## 2. Aristotle on Orexis (Desire / ὄρεξις) If phantasia furnishes the representational content upon which the animal acts, it is orexis — desire in its broadest sense — that supplies the motive force. Aristotle is emphatic that no animal moves without desire; the phantasma, however vivid, cannot by itself produce locomotion. Thus the circuit from phantasia to kinesis necessarily passes through orexis, and it is this intermediate moment that we must now examine. Desire, for Aristotle, is not a single homogeneous impulse but admits of several species: epithumia (appetite), thumos (spirited emotion), and boulēsis (rational wish). Each of these species is connected to a different grade of phantasia — appetite to sensitive phantasia, rational wish to deliberative phantasia — and it is perhaps in the differentiation of desire that we see most clearly how the psychological architecture of *De Anima* III.9–11 maps onto the biological observations of *De Motu Animalium*. The affective dimension of desire is richly elaborated in Aristotle's account of the corporeal concomitants of emotion. In *De Motu Animalium*, (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) "blind courage and panic fears, erotic motions, and the rest of the corporeal affections, pleasant and painful, are all accompanied by heating or chilling, some in a particular member, others in the body generally" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, pp. 8–9). This passage is crucial because orexis is not merely a psychological state but has immediate physiological manifestation; the heating and chilling of the body are not incidental accompaniments but constitutive elements of the desiderative process by which phantasia issues in movement. Similarly, (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) the same treatise that "thinking and imagination, as we said above, produce that which brings about the affections, since they produce the forms which bring them about" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). Hence the relationship between phantasia and orexis is not one of mere temporal succession — first the image, then the desire — but of formal causation: the phantasma produces the form that is the affection, and this affection, experienced as pleasure or pain, constitutes the desire that initiates movement. Heidegger's reading of Aristotelian πάθη illuminates this point from a different angle. In his *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, Heidegger insists that these "affects" (πάθη) "are not states pertaining to ensouled things, but are concerned with a disposition of living things in their world, in the mode of being positioned toward something, allowing a matter to matter to it" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 96–98). This characterization reframes orexis not as an inner psychological event that subsequently causes an outer bodily response but as a mode of being-in-the-world in which the animal is already oriented toward something that matters to it. Accordingly, the Heideggerian desire, for Aristotle, belongs to the totality of involvements that constitute the animal's environment; the object of desire is not a neutral stimulus but something that solicits the animal precisely because of the animal's constitutive openness to its world. The implications for the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit are significant: if desire is a mode of disposition rather than a discrete psychological state, then the passage from phantasia to kinesis through orexis is not a causal chain of separable events but a unitary structure of animal comportment. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) practical deliberation about what to pursue depends upon the assessment of what is "practicable" and what "surpasses another," noting that practicable things are "those in which everyone, or most people, or one's equals, or one's inferiors have succeeded" and that "a thing which surpasses another may be regarded as being that other thing plus something more" (Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, p. 18). While this passage belongs to the rhetorical context of deliberation about goods, it nonetheless reveals the evaluative structure that underlies deliberative phantasia; for it is precisely by measuring one phantasma against another — determining which represents the greater good — that the calculative animal arrives at a determinate desire and, subsequently, at action. The rhetorical analysis thus supplements the psychological account of *De Anima* by making explicit the comparative logic that governs deliberative orexis. 

## 3. Aristotle on Kinesis (Movement / Change / κίνησις) The culmination of the phantasia-orexis circuit is kinesis — the actual locomotive movement of the animal. Yet kinesis, in Aristotle's broader ontological framework, is not limited to animal locomotion; it designates the actuality of the potential qua potential, and it is this general concept that undergirds the specific analysis of animal movement in *De Motu Animalium*. Aristotle opens that treatise by announcing that "there remains an investigation of the common cause of any sort of animal movement whatsoever" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 1). The search for a "common cause" signals that Aristotle intends to identify a single explanatory structure — a schema applicable to all animals, whether they fly, swim, or walk — and it is the phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit that provides this structure. Indeed, the practical syllogism, in which the major general desire and the minor premiss supplies a particular phantasma of the present situation, is the logical form that Aristotle assigns to the generation of animal movement; the conclusion of the syllogism is the action itself. Heidegger's interpretation of Aristotelian κίνησις provides essential ontological clarification. In *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, Heidegger discusses the relational character of movement, observing that "the being-context about which I say, 'the being is in movement,' is determined by the category of the πρός τι, the 'being-in-relation-to-an-other,' namely, the moving thing characterized by ποίησις, the moved thing by πάθησις" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 232). Accordingly, movement is not a property of a single substance considered in isolation but a relational determination involving both agent and patient — ποίησις and πάθησις as two modes of being-present in relation to movement. When applied to animal locomotion, this relational analysis implies that the moving animal stands in a constitutive relation to its environment; the object of desire, presented through phantasia, is the "other" toward which the animal is in relation, and the movement is the actualization of the potential inherent in that relation. Hence, kinesis is not merely a physical displacement but an ontological event that discloses the animal's being-in-relation-to its world. Furthermore, Heidegger draws attention to the connection between ἐνέργεια and κίνησις, noting that "ἐνέργεια, specifically, is related in itself πρὸς τὴν ἐντελέχειαν" and that the name ἐνέργεια "came to be carried over to the other, to what contrasted with determinations of movement" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 213–215). For animal kinesis, this means that the movement toward the desired object is structured teleologically: the animal moves because the phantasma presents an end (a τέλος) that the animal has not yet achieved, and the movement is the process of achieving it. The practical syllogism, in this light, is not merely a logical device but the articulation of the teleological structure of animal movement itself. The physiological dimension of kinesis completes the picture. (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]) in *De Motu Animalium*, the parts of the body that display locomotive motion most conspicuously "each is in a sense a separate animal, the reason being that each contains vital moisture" (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). The heart, which "contains the origins of the senses," is the physiological locus where the phantasmata produce their affective and locomotive effects (Aristotle, *Movement Of Animals*, p. 11). Thus the circuit from phantasia through orexis to kinesis is at once psychological and physiological: the phantasma produces a form that alters the temperature and moisture of the heart and the relevant bodily members, and this alteration constitutes the bodily movement. The sense-perception that gave rise to the phantasia is itself a process of being affected — (Aristotle 2014, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), "all sense-perception is a process of being so affected; so that that which makes something such as it itself actually is makes the other such because the other is already potentially such" (Aristotle, *On The Soul (De Anima)*, p. 36). Similarly, the kinesis of animal locomotion is a process of being affected by the phantasma through the medium of desire, completing the explanatory circuit that *De Anima* III.9–11 and *De Motu Animalium* 6–8 jointly articulate. 

## 4. Conclusion The phantasia-orexis-kinesis circuit constitutes one of Aristotle's most elegant explanatory achievements, unifying the psychological, physiological, and ontological dimensions of animal action within a single integrated framework. Phantasia, as a movement arising from actual sensation, furnishes the representational content — the phantasma — that makes the absent object present to the animal; orexis, aroused by the pleasant or painful character of the phantasma, supplies the motive force that drives the animal toward or away from the represented object; and kinesis, the actualization of the potential inherent in the animal's relation to its environment, constitutes the locomotive act itself. The distinction between sensitive and deliberative phantasia ensures that the framework applies differentially to rational and non-rational animals, while the relational ontology of κίνησις — as Heidegger has helped us to see — situates animal movement within the broader context of being-in-relation-to-an-other. The corporeal affections that accompany desire — the heating and chilling, the alterations of the heart — ground the psychological circuit in the material reality of the living body. Perhaps the deepest insight of this account is that the passage from phantasia to kinesis through orexis is not a causal chain of discrete events but a unitary structure in which the animal, disposed toward its world, is moved by what matters to it. --- # VALIDATION APPENDIX ## Claim Map | # | Claim | Source | Page(s) |
